extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers and scholars interested in American short fiction anthologies
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions of the selection history, editorial practice, and implicit standards used by The Best American Short Stories anthology series; useful for understanding what kinds of short stories and editorial choices the series favors. Covers historical editors' preferences, the post-1978 selection procedure, and attention to new currents/minority literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Brien's three-star ranking (literary permanence)
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien's editions contained lengthy tabulations of stories and magazines, ranked on a scale of three stars (representing O'Brien's notion of their "literary permanence").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: O'Brien claimed to read around 8,000 stories a year and used the rankings to indicate which works he believed had lasting literary value. This is an explicit scoring/annotation system: three-star as an indicator of perceived permanence. Surrounding commentary notes that his tastes were sometimes seen as snobbish or pedantic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for consciously literary stories (avoid formulaic/sentimental commercial fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien was deeply and vocally skeptical of the value of commercial short fiction, which tended to the formulaic and sentimental; he insisted on the need for a consciously literary development of the short story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection under O'Brien favored stories that advanced literary craft and experimentation rather than popular, formula-driven pieces. Anti-patterns: sentimental, formulaic commercial fiction. Examples: O'Brien used selections to draw attention to emerging serious writers (e.g., anthologizing early Hemingway).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process: series editor recommends 120; guest editor selects 20
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1978 the editor would choose the best twenty stories from 120 stories recommended by the series editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural/quality-control standard: the series editor curates a longlist (~120) and a guest editor (each year) makes the final selection of ~20. Scoring guidance implicit: stories must first be strong enough to make the 120 recommended list to be eligible. Note: guest editors have sometimes gone beyond the series editor's recommendations (example: John Gardner in 1982).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest editor should be a writer of reputation who selects and introduces the volume
rubrics_metrics.description: A different writer of reputation would select the contents and introduce the volume each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial authority and taste of a reputable guest editor is an explicit part of the series' standard; the guest editor's selections and introduction shape the anthology's voice and criteria for 'best.' The page lists decades of named guest editors to show the prestige and influence of that role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness and inclusion of new currents and minority literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors (for example Martha Foley) attended to the rise of so-called minority literature, dedicating volumes (e.g., the 1975 volume to Leslie Marmon Silko), though it has been argued the series was sometimes less perceptive in this area than it might have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: responsiveness to new literary currents and inclusion of minority voices is part of the anthology's evolving standards. Guidance/limitation: historical practice shows some attention but also criticism that the series did not always perceptively represent these currents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthology selections function as a 'running judgment' of tastes across decades
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual volumes provide a running judgement of tastes regarding short stories across the decades: 'These were the stories that judges in the 1930's, 40's and 50's chose. We get a sense of how we and our writers have changed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard: selections are contextual and reflective of the contemporary judges' tastes rather than an absolute, ahistorical canon. Use this when evaluating inclusion: a story's selection signals contemporaneous critical taste as much as intrinsic, timeless quality.
